summary: Specifies linear protection switching for MPLS-TP networks, supporting the capabilities of a packet transport network as defined by the ITU-T. It is a joint IETF and ITU-T effort and covers protection against failures along a path.

plainLanguage.summary: If the main path breaks, traffic quickly switches to a spare path set up in advance. This explains how that fast switching works for MPLS-TP.

subtitle: A small protocol that lets the two ends of an MPLS-TP path agree, within milliseconds, to move traffic to a backup path.

tldr.problem: When a working path fails, both ends of a bidirectional path must switch to the protection path together, or traffic is lost or sent the wrong way.
tldr.mechanism: The Protection State Coordination (PSC) protocol sends small messages over the protection path. They carry a request, a fault path and a data path, and each end runs a state machine that ranks local triggers and remote messages by priority.
tldr.outcome: Ends switch without waiting for an acknowledgement and converge once the messages arrive. The RFC recommends rapid messages no more than 3.3 ms apart to reach switching within 50 ms.

today: RFC 6378 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7214, RFC 7271 and RFC 7324; it has not been obsoleted. Read those updates together with this RFC.

sections.title: Why Linear Protection Needs Coordination
sections.content:
This RFC is part of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort to give MPLS a Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) that supports a packet transport network as the ITU-T defines it. It defines a protocol that can serve as the Protection State Coordination (PSC) function for linear protection, which the MPLS-TP Survivability Framework in RFC 6372 describes.

Linear protection works between any pair of points in a mesh network. It can protect against a defect in an intermediate node, a span, a transport path segment or an end-to-end transport path. It is a fast and simple survivability mechanism.

Protection switching is applied to a protection domain. For a point-to-point LSP this is two Label Edge Routers (LERs) and the transport paths that connect them. Bidirectional protection needs both ends to agree which path carries traffic, which is what this protocol is for.
sections.plainLanguage: A road has a main lane and a spare lane. If the main lane breaks, the two ends of the road must pick the spare lane together.

sections.title: Protection Architectures and Scope
sections.content:
Protection is fully allocated: the route and resources of the protection path are reserved for the working path or paths it protects.

  • 1+1: a protection path is dedicated to the working path. A permanent bridge at the source feeds traffic to both paths, and a selector at the sink chooses one. Bidirectional switching needs the PSC protocol.
  • 1:1: traffic goes on either the working or the protection path, using a selector at the source. A selector at the sink picks the path, so both ends must be coordinated.
  • 1:n: like 1:1, but the protection path is shared among n services. Coordination and resource allocation for this are for further study.

The basic protocol is designed for 1:1 protection, bidirectional protection, and 1+1 protection of a bidirectional path (with unidirectional or bidirectional switching). 1:1 unidirectional, 1:n and point-to-multipoint uses are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: With 1+1 you always send a copy down both roads. With 1:1 you use one road at a time, and with 1:n several roads share one spare.

sections.title: Local Requests and the Control Logic
sections.content:
The control logic is split into pieces for description only. The Local Request logic takes triggers from five sources, picks the highest priority, and hands one current local request to the PSC Control logic. That logic compares it with the request received from the far-end LER and the current state, decides what to do, and tells the Message Generator what to send.

  • Operator commands: Forced Switch, Manual Switch, Clear and Lockout of protection MUST be supported.
  • Server-layer alarms: may be controlled by a configurable hold-off timer.
  • Control plane indications: MAY trigger switching.
  • OAM indications: detect failure or degrade on either path and MUST be passed to the Local Request logic.
  • WTR Expires: from the Wait-to-Restore timer.

Outputs are Clear, Lockout (LO), Signal Fail (SF), Signal Degrade (SD), Clear Signal Fail (SFc), Forced Switch (FS), Manual Switch (MS), WTR Expires and No Request (NR). Signal Degrade handling is a placeholder for a future document.

In 1+1 unidirectional protection, an LER that receives a remote request SHALL NOT switch its selector.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end has a helper who listens to alarms, the boss's orders and a timer, then tells a decision-maker only the most important thing.

sections.title: Protection States and the Wait-to-Restore Timer
sections.content:
Each LER keeps the state of the protection domain, why it is in that state, and whether the state is local (caused by a local input) or remote (caused by a PSC message). If both apply, the state is local. The states are:

  • Normal: traffic on the working path and no trigger events.
  • Unavailable: the protection path is unusable because of a Lockout or a failure on it.
  • Protecting failure: the working path failed and traffic uses the protection path.
  • Protecting administrative: an operator command moved traffic to the protection path.
  • Wait-to-Restore: recovering from a working path failure, held by the WTR timer.
  • Do-not-Revert: recovered, but the operator configured no automatic reversion.

The WTR timer prevents flapping from an intermittent fault. It is Running or Stopped. If it expires, it generates WTR Expires. Stopping it resets it without generating that signal. The RFC defines the reaction of each state to each local input and remote message in detail, and Appendix A gives the state tables.
sections.plainLanguage: After the main road is fixed, you wait a bit to be sure it will stay fixed before going back. That waiting is the timer.

sections.title: The PSC Message
sections.content:
PSC messages travel over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) with channel type PSC-CT=0x0024. The payload has these fields: Ver (value 1), Request (4 bits), PT (protection type), R (revertive), FPath (fault path), Path (data path), TLV Length (0 for the basic protocol) and optional TLVs. Reserved fields MUST be 0 and are ignored on receipt.

PT is 3 for bidirectional switching with a permanent bridge, 2 for bidirectional with a selector bridge and 1 for unidirectional with a permanent bridge. Inconsistent ends trigger an alarm to the management system. R is 1 for revertive and 0 for non-revertive; a mismatch SHOULD be reported to management.

FPath is 0 when the anomaly is on the protection path and 1 when it is on the working path. Path is 0 when the protection path carries no user traffic (or only redundant copies in 1+1), and 1 when it carries the traffic that used the working path.

The RFC writes messages as REQ(FPath, Path). For example, a local Signal Fail on the working path from Normal state sends SF(1,1), and Normal state sends NR(0,0). IANA registered the channel type and created registries for the Request field and TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is a tiny note with a few boxes: what happened, which road is broken, and which road the cars are on now.

sections.title: Priorities and Message Timing
sections.content:
PSC messages SHALL be sent on the protection path only, which avoids disturbing normal traffic and avoids races. When the state changes because of a local input, three messages SHALL be sent as quickly as possible, so a lost one or two does not matter. After that the LER MUST keep repeating the latest message. For switching within 50 ms, the first three SHOULD be no more than 3.3 ms apart, which lets the far end receive the trigger within 10 ms. Later messages SHOULD default to every 5 seconds, to show the session is alive.

Local requests rank from highest to lowest: Clear, Lockout, Forced Switch, Signal Fail on protection, Signal Fail on working, Signal Degrade, Clear Signal Fail/Degrade, Manual Switch, WTR Expires, No Request. A remote message ranks just below the matching local one. Only the highest priority input drives the state.

The protocol is single-phased: an end switches and tells its peer without waiting for an acknowledgement. For a short time the ends may use different paths until the remote message arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, you shout three times quickly in case someone misses it, then check in every so often to show you are still there.

sections.title: Security of the Associated Channel
sections.content:
MPLS-TP builds on MPLS security assumptions: injecting traffic into the network is very hard. Since PSC runs in the G-ACh, it depends on the security of that channel. Changing control messages requires subverting a transit node, which the RFC says is hard and cannot be prevented at the protocol level; management techniques are more appropriate.

A new concern is accidental corruption of the Request, FPath or Path fields, which would change the peer's behavior. The RFC offers no way to prevent a change in behavior, but states that the state transitions converge on a known and stable behavior if messages do not match reality. The G-ACh can also be a covert channel, and transit nodes SHOULD NOT police it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is hard for a stranger to sneak notes into this system, but a smudged note could confuse one end. The rules are built so things settle down anyway.
